summaries.summary: The extension is a functional ad-injector targeting the Cursor AI coding editor. It is not malicious in the traditional sense (no credential theft, no remote shell, no ransomware), but it is highly suspicious due to its deceptive nature. It injects code into a third-party application's UI to display ads, tracks user interactions (clicks, view time), and sends this telemetry to a backend. The 'persistence_evasion' flags are false positives related to the Page Visibility API. The primary risk is the unauthorized modification of the host application's UI and the collection of user activity data for advertising purposes, which may violate user expectations and potentially the host app's terms of service.

The extension 'Greedy Krab' is a sophisticated ad-injection tool that targets the 'Codex' AI coding extension. It employs a supply-chain attack pattern by injecting an IIFE into the target's internal React component tree to overlay advertisements on the 'Thinking' status indicator. While the code itself does not contain obvious malware payloads like keyloggers or credential stealers, it engages in aggressive UI hijacking, unauthorized DOM manipulation, and telemetry exfiltration to third-party servers. The use of `onStartupFinished` and the complexity of the injection logic (bypassing CSP via loopback proxies, precise DOM targeting) indicate a high level of sophistication and potential for abuse, warranting a SUSPICIOUS verdict due to the deceptive nature of its operation within another extension's environment.

findings.description: The extension claims to display ads in 'compatible AI coding tool interfaces' but the code explicitly targets and injects itself into Cursor's internal React component tree (`ThinkingShimmer`). It uses hardcoded CSS selectors (`[class*="composer-loading"]`, etc.) to locate specific UI elements. This is a form of UI hijacking/overlay injection, which is deceptive and potentially violates the terms of service of the host application (Cursor).
findings.code_reference: var CURSOR_THINKING_SEL = '[class*="composer-loading"], [class*="generating"], [data-thinking]'; ... function findRow() { var els = document.querySelectorAll(CURSOR_THINKING_SEL); ... }

findings.description: The code collects telemetry data including `location.href` (slice), click events, view durations, and ad IDs. This data is sent via `fetch` to a local loopback address (`http://127.0.0.1:...`) which acts as a proxy for the external backend (`greedykrab-backend...`). While the destination is local, the data collected (especially `location.href` and interaction patterns) constitutes user activity monitoring.
findings.code_reference: function dlog(evt, data) { ... fetch(BASE + "/log", { method: "POST", ... body: JSON.stringify(o) }) ... }

findings.description: The code dynamically creates DOM elements (`div`, `a`, `svg`) and injects them into the `document.body` with high z-index (`2147483646`) to overlay the host application's UI. It constructs clickable links (`<a href="...">`) that direct users to external advertising URLs. This is the core functionality of an adware extension.
findings.code_reference: function buildAd(dots, elapsed) { ... var A = '<a href="' + href + '" target="_blank" ... data-greedykrab-ad="1" ...>' ... }

findings.description: The static scanner flagged 'persistence_evasion' due to the string `.hidden`. In this context, it refers to `document.hidden` (the Page Visibility API) used to pause ad billing when the tab is not visible. This is a legitimate optimization for ad-tech, not an attempt to hide files or processes.
findings.code_reference: var hidden = false; try { hidden = (typeof document.hidden === "boolean") && document.hidden; } catch (e) { hidden = false; }

findings.description: The extension claims to be an ad-revenue sharing tool ('Greedy Krab') but injects code directly into the internal React component tree of 'Codex' (an AI coding tool). The code explicitly states it patches the 'ThinkingShimmer' entry to inject an overlay. This is a supply-chain attack vector where the extension modifies the behavior of another installed extension/application without explicit user consent for that specific modification, potentially violating VS Code's extension isolation principles.
findings.code_reference: Injects as the first statement of Codex's ThinkingShimmer entry... We do NOT swap e.message... Instead... we read Codex's thinking row READ-ONLY and paint the ad in OUR OWN element appended to <body>

findings.description: The extension uses `onStartupFinished` activation event. For an ad-display extension, this is aggressive and ensures the code runs immediately upon VS Code startup, potentially before the user has interacted with the specific AI tool. This increases the attack surface and persistence.

The code sends telemetry and billing data to a local loopback server (`http://127.0.0.1:...`) which likely proxies to `greedykrab-backend-402535524137.asia` or `update.greedykrab.net`. The data includes `location.href` (slice), `className`, and detailed view-time metrics. While labeled as 'billing', this constitutes exfiltration of user activity patterns and potentially sensitive context (URLs) to third-party servers.

The code aggressively manipulates the DOM by creating a fixed-position overlay (`z-index:2147483646`) that sits on top of the AI tool's UI. It uses `requestAnimationFrame` and `setInterval` to continuously poll for specific CSS classes (`text-size-chat`, `loading-shimmer`) to determine when to show the ad. This is a form of UI hijacking.

The static scanner flagged `.hidden` attribute usage. In this context, it is used for CSS visibility (`visibility:hidden`) and DOM state checks (`document.hidden`), not for setting file system hidden attributes. This is a false positive for file system evasion, but the technique of hiding the overlay until it is 'visible' is part of the ad injection logic.
